title: RAG pipeline from scratch
summary: Build a complete retrieval-augmented generation system end-to-end: chunking, embeddings, vector search, generation, and evaluation. A 6-week capstone for ML engineers who want to understand the full stack.
contentIntro:
## What you'll build

A working RAG system over a corpus of your choice — typically the documentation for a tool you use, a set of research papers, or a company knowledge base. By the end, you'll have:

- A chunking + embedding pipeline that turns documents into a searchable vector index
- A retriever with reranking
- A generator with prompt assembly + citation
- An evaluation harness that lets you compare system variants

The goal isn't to recreate LangChain. The goal is to build every piece yourself so you understand the failure modes of each.

contentUndergrad:
## What you'll build

A production-shaped RAG system, written by you. Five milestones, ~6 weeks, ~10-15 hours per week.

## Format

Each milestone has:
- A deliverable (code in a GitHub repo + a writeup explaining your decisions)
- A rubric the AI grader uses to score correctness, depth, and engineering judgment
- Optional runnable tests for the algorithmic milestones

When all five pass, your public artifact page goes live. Use it as portfolio; the signed transcript is independently verifiable.

## Why this capstone

RAG is the dominant pattern for grounding LLM outputs. Every production deployment uses some variant. The difference between a good and bad RAG system is not the LLM — it's the chunking, retrieval, reranking, and eval choices that build up around it. By the end of this capstone, you'll have made every one of those choices yourself.

contentGrad:
## What you'll build

A RAG system with the production discipline of a serving deployment: chunking strategy validated against retrieval evals, hybrid retrieval (vector + lexical), cross-encoder reranking, faithfulness scoring, and ablation studies on every component.

Defense (claim-thread Q&A on the artifact page) is part of the rubric. Be ready to argue why your chunking strategy beat the alternatives, what your retrieval-eval set looks like, and where your system still fails.

[[rag]] · [[retrieval-evaluation]] · [[preference-optimization]]

milestones.title: Chunking + embedding store
milestones.description:
Build the document ingestion pipeline.

- Pick a corpus (research papers, docs for a tool you use, etc.) — at least 50 documents
- Chunk: write a chunker that splits on semantic boundaries (sections, paragraphs) with overlap. Compare 2-3 chunk sizes empirically.
- Embed: pick an open embedding model (sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 or BGE) and embed every chunk
- Store: index the chunks in any vector store (FAISS, Chroma, pgvector, or just numpy + cosine similarity)

In your writeup: explain *why* you picked your chunk size. Show a small ablation: how does retrieval quality change as chunk size varies? You'll need a small eval set (10-20 questions with expected chunks) to measure this — building that set is part of the milestone.

criteria.description: Chunking + embedding + storage pipeline works end-to-end on the chosen corpus.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the artifacts demonstrate a working ingestion pipeline: chunking with overlap, embedding via a real model, indexing in a vector store. Does the writeup show an actual run on a real corpus?

criteria.description: Chunk-size ablation with a small evaluation set.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score the rigor of the chunk-size comparison. Did the learner build an eval set (even small) and measure how chunk size affects retrieval? Did they reach a defended conclusion?
Score the writeup's depth on chunking strategy and embedding model choice.

milestones.title: Retrieval (vector search + reranker)
milestones.description:
Build a two-stage retrieval pipeline.

- **Stage 1**: vector search returns top-50 candidates by cosine similarity
- **Stage 2**: cross-encoder rerank the top-50 down to top-5

Use any open cross-encoder (BAAI/bge-reranker-base, ms-marco-MiniLM, or Cohere Rerank if you have an API key). Build a small eval set of (query, expected-relevant-chunks) pairs and measure:

- Hit rate @ top-5 with vector-only
- Hit rate @ top-5 with vector + rerank
- MRR for both

In your writeup: report the delta. Reranking should give a measurable lift; quantify it. If it doesn't help, explain why (small corpus, queries already match embeddings well).

criteria.description: Two-stage retrieval works end-to-end with a real cross-encoder reranker.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the retrieval pipeline correctly implements both stages — vector search + cross-encoder reranking — and produces sensible results on the chosen corpus.

criteria.description: Eval set + retrieval metrics (hit rate, MRR) reported.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score the rigor of the retrieval evaluation. Are hit rate and MRR computed on a real eval set? Is the vector-only vs. vector+rerank delta quantified?

criteria.description: Analysis of when reranking helps and when it doesn't.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score the writeup's depth on the role of reranking. Does the learner explain *why* the cross-encoder helps (or doesn't) for their corpus and query distribution?

milestones.title: Generation with citations
milestones.description:
Wire the retriever to an LLM.

- Assemble a prompt: `[system prompt with citation instruction] + [retrieved chunks with chunk IDs] + [user query]`
- Generate with any LLM (open: LLaMA-3-8B; API: GPT-4o-mini or Claude Haiku)
- Parse the model's output to extract citations and verify they reference real chunk IDs
- If a generated answer cites chunks that weren't in the retrieved set, flag it as a faithfulness failure

In your writeup: show 5-10 example queries with the assembled prompt, the model's answer, and the citation correctness check. At least one should be a failure case (the model citing wrongly or hallucinating beyond the chunks). Discuss what you'd do to mitigate.

criteria.description: Generation pipeline assembles prompts correctly and verifies citations.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the generation pipeline correctly assembles retrieved chunks into a prompt, generates answers, and verifies citations against the retrieved set.

criteria.description: Demonstrates and analyzes failure modes (hallucination, mis-citation).
criteria.aiPrompt: Score the depth of the failure-mode analysis. Does the learner show real failure cases? Do they propose mitigations (better retrieval, prompt changes, smaller chunks)?
Score the writeup's clarity on showing concrete example queries through the pipeline.

milestones.title: End-to-end evaluation harness
milestones.description:
Build a harness that scores the entire system on:

- **Faithfulness**: does the generated answer say only things supported by retrieved chunks? (LLM-as-judge or RAGAS-style)
- **Answer relevance**: does the answer address the query? (LLM-as-judge)
- **Context recall**: did retrieval surface enough context to answer correctly? (LLM-as-judge with ground truth)

Use a framework like RAGAS or roll your own. Run it on at least 30 queries.

In your writeup: present the metrics for the system as a whole + an ablation showing how each component contributes. Specifically, what happens if you skip the reranker? What happens if you halve the number of retrieved chunks?

criteria.description: End-to-end eval harness runs and produces sensible metrics.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the eval harness correctly implements faithfulness / answer-relevance / context-recall metrics and runs on a non-trivial test set.
Score the rigor of the component ablation. Are at least two ablations (e.g., no rerank, fewer chunks, different embed model) reported? Are the deltas quantified?
Score the writeup's depth on what each metric measures and where the system is bottlenecked.

milestones.title: Production write-up + deployment notes
milestones.description:
Document the system as if you were handing it off to another engineer.

In your final writeup, cover:

- **Architecture diagram**: chunking → embedding → vector store → retrieval → reranking → generation → eval
- **Resource footprint**: how much memory does the index take? How long is the typical query latency? How does it scale with corpus size?
- **Failure modes you found**: what fails reliably? What's brittle?
- **What you'd change**: if you had another month, what would you improve, and why
- **Honest limitations**: what kinds of queries does the system handle poorly?

This is the milestone where you demonstrate engineering judgment. The grader scores on completeness and honesty more than on numerical results.

criteria.description: Covers architecture, resources, failure modes, and limitations.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the writeup covers all required sections: architecture, resource footprint, failure modes, proposed improvements, and honest limitations.
Score the depth of engineering judgment shown. Does the learner identify real failure modes? Do their proposed improvements show understanding of the system's bottlenecks?
Score whether the writeup honestly describes what the system does poorly, not just what works.
